quests.instruction: You jump up fast after lying on the floor, and everything seems to swirl for a moment. Blood needs a second to catch up to which part?
quests.hint: It is the part that feels dizzy.
quests.explanation: When you stand up fast, gravity pulls blood down toward your legs for a moment, so the brain briefly gets a little less. Your body quickly corrects it.
quests.funFact: Standing up slowly gives your blood vessels time to tighten and send blood upward.

quests.instruction: You gulp a frozen drink, and a sudden headache stabs your forehead. Something very cold touching which part of your mouth can cause this brain freeze?
quests.hint: It is the ceiling of your mouth.
quests.explanation: The cold makes blood vessels near the roof of your mouth tighten and then widen again, and the nerves send a pain message that feels like it comes from your head.
quests.funFact: Brain freeze usually fades in under a minute, and sipping slowly helps you avoid it.

quests.instruction: You sit cross-legged for a long time, and your foot goes tingly and numb, as if it has fallen asleep. What was pressed, so its messages were blocked for a while?
quests.hint: They carry messages between your foot and your brain.
quests.explanation: Pressure squeezed the nerves in your leg, so their messages could not get through. When you move, they start working again, and the tingling is that restart.
quests.funFact: The tingly feeling is often called pins and needles.

quests.instruction: At a check-up, a nurse takes a little blood from a vein, usually on the inside of which joint, because the veins are easy to find there?
quests.hint: It is the hinge between your upper arm and your forearm.
quests.explanation: Veins run close to the skin on the inside of the elbow, so a nurse can reach one easily.
quests.funFact: A small blood sample can tell doctors about many things, from how well your blood carries oxygen to whether you are fighting an infection.

quests.instruction: A doctor listens to your breathing with a stethoscope placed on your back, not only your chest. Which organs is the doctor listening to?
quests.hint: They are the organs that fill with air as you breathe.
quests.explanation: Your lungs reach around to your back, so a doctor can hear the airflow from behind.
quests.funFact: Each lung stretches from just above your collarbone down to the bottom of your rib cage.

quests.instruction: Vaccine shots are often given in the muscle at the top of the upper arm. Which joint sits just under that muscle?
quests.hint: It is the joint that lets your arm swing in circles.
quests.explanation: The muscle at the top of the arm, called the deltoid, covers the shoulder joint and is a convenient place for a shot.
quests.funFact: A muscle has a good blood supply, so the body can start using the medicine soon.

quests.instruction: After a hot game when you forgot to drink, your pee looks darker than usual. Which organs are holding on to extra water by making stronger pee?
quests.hint: They clean your blood and control how much water leaves your body.
quests.explanation: When your body needs water, the kidneys keep more of it and make darker, stronger pee. Drinking water helps.
quests.funFact: Pale yellow pee usually means you are drinking enough.

quests.instruction: After a fizzy drink, a gas bubble comes up as a burp. Which part held that gas?
quests.hint: It is where your drink goes after you swallow.
quests.explanation: Fizzy drinks release gas, and extra air can collect in the stomach until it comes back up the food pipe.
quests.funFact: The bubbles in soda are carbon dioxide gas.

quests.instruction: You accidentally swallow a piece of chewing gum. Which parts push it along, with the leftovers, until it leaves your body?
quests.hint: They squeeze food along inside your tummy.
quests.explanation: Gum is not digested, but it moves through the intestines like other leftovers and leaves in a few days.
quests.funFact: The old idea that gum stays in your stomach for seven years is a myth.

quests.instruction: At first, a dark movie theater looks black, but after a few minutes you can see the seats. Which layer at the back of your eye becomes more sensitive?
quests.hint: It is the layer that catches light.
quests.explanation: In the dark, the retina slowly becomes more sensitive, which is why your sight improves over a few minutes.
quests.funFact: Full adjustment to the dark can take 20 to 30 minutes.

quests.instruction: Your own voice sounds strange on a recording, because when you talk, it also travels to your ears through which parts of your head?
quests.hint: They carry vibrations well.
quests.explanation: When you speak, vibrations travel through the bones of your skull as well as through the air, so your voice sounds fuller to you than it does to others.
quests.funFact: A recording lets you hear your voice the way other people hear it, only through the air.

quests.instruction: You cannot tickle yourself, because a part of your brain predicts your own touch and cancels it. Which part does the predicting?
quests.hint: It is the part that helps with smooth movement.
quests.explanation: The cerebellum predicts what your own movements will feel like, so your own touch is not surprising or ticklish.
quests.funFact: A tickle machine can tickle you, because your brain cannot predict its touch as well.

quests.instruction: After a fast run, your cheeks turn red as tiny tubes under the skin widen to let heat escape. What are those tubes?
quests.hint: They carry blood close to the surface.
quests.explanation: When you are hot, blood vessels near the skin widen, which brings more blood to the surface so heat can escape.
quests.funFact: In the cold, those vessels narrow to keep warmth inside.

quests.instruction: On a cold morning, you can see your breath like a small cloud. Which parts make that warm, damp air?
quests.hint: You breathe out from them.
quests.explanation: The air you breathe out is warm and damp, and in cold air the moisture turns into tiny droplets you can see.
quests.funFact: Your breath is just as damp in summer, but the warm air hides the droplets.

quests.instruction: Pollen floats by, and your nose runs and your eyes itch. Which body system is reacting to a harmless thing as if it were a germ?
quests.hint: It is the system that protects you from germs.
quests.explanation: In an allergy, the immune system overreacts to something harmless, such as pollen, and makes you sneeze or itch.
quests.funFact: Allergies are very common in children.

quests.instruction: Which organ helps break down medicines and other substances that enter your body, one reason to take medicine only from a trusted grown-up?
quests.hint: It sits under your ribs on the right and works like a filter.
quests.explanation: The liver breaks down many substances, including medicines, so taking too much can overload it.
quests.funFact: The liver does hundreds of jobs, from making bile to storing energy.

quests.instruction: If you skip breakfast, it can be harder to concentrate in class. Which part runs mostly on sugar from your blood?
quests.hint: It stores very little energy of its own.
quests.explanation: The brain depends on a steady supply of sugar from the blood, so a healthy breakfast helps it work well.
quests.funFact: Your brain makes up about two percent of your body weight, but it uses a much bigger share of your energy.

quests.instruction: A crumb goes down the wrong way, and you cough hard. Which tube are you protecting?
quests.hint: It carries air to your lungs.
quests.explanation: Coughing blasts air out to clear anything that does not belong in the windpipe.
quests.funFact: A cough is a reflex, so it happens before you decide to cough.

quests.instruction: A person who uses a wheelchair often moves it by pushing the wheels with strong muscles in which parts?
quests.hint: Shoulders and biceps are part of them.
quests.explanation: Pushing a wheelchair uses the muscles of the shoulders and arms, so many wheelchair users have very strong ones.
quests.funFact: Wheelchair sports such as basketball and racing are played at the Paralympic Games.

quests.instruction: A friend who reads lips needs to see your mouth clearly. Which part of your body should you turn toward them when you talk?
quests.hint: It is the part people look at when you speak.
quests.explanation: Facing a person who lip-reads, speaking clearly, and not covering your mouth all help them understand you.
quests.funFact: Only some speech sounds can be seen on the lips, so lip readers also use clues from the face and the situation.

quests.instruction: Braces gently push which parts into new positions over many months?
quests.hint: They are lined up in rows.
quests.explanation: Braces apply gentle pressure, and the bone around each tooth slowly rebuilds so that the tooth settles into its new place.
quests.funFact: Many people wear braces for one to three years.

quests.instruction: Going down a slide, which part of your body should go first so your head stays safe?
quests.hint: Your legs lead the way.
quests.explanation: Going feet first lets your legs absorb the bump at the bottom and keeps your head out of the way.
quests.funFact: Sitting upright, not lying down or going headfirst, is the safest way down.

quests.instruction: After climbing a rope wall, which part of your arms feels tired and tight from gripping so hard?
quests.hint: Its muscles help you grip and twist.
quests.explanation: Gripping uses muscles in the forearm, which pull on tendons that reach your fingers.
quests.funFact: Climbers train their forearms and fingers to hold on for a long time.

quests.instruction: You sit with your legs straight and reach for your toes. Which muscles at the back of your thighs feel the stretch?
quests.hint: They help bend your knee.
quests.explanation: The hamstrings run down the back of the thigh, so reaching forward with straight knees stretches them.
quests.funFact: People who sit for long periods often have tight hamstrings.

quests.instruction: A bat flies in total darkness by listening to echoes of its own squeaks. Which body part does it rely on most?
quests.hint: Many bats have big, folded ones.
quests.explanation: Bats send out high squeaks and use their ears to catch the echoes, which tell them where objects are.
quests.funFact: This echo sensing is called echolocation, and dolphins use it, too.

quests.instruction: A snake keeps flicking out a forked part of its body to pick up scent particles from the air. Which part is it?
quests.hint: It flicks in and out of the mouth.
quests.explanation: The forked tongue collects scent particles and brings them back to sensors in the roof of the mouth.
quests.funFact: The fork lets a snake tell which side a smell is stronger on, a bit like having two noses.

quests.instruction: An elephant's trunk is a very long version of which human body part, joined with the upper lip?
quests.hint: You smell with it.
quests.explanation: An elephant's trunk is a long nose and upper lip together, used for smelling, breathing, drinking, and grabbing.
quests.funFact: An elephant's trunk contains about 40,000 muscles.

quests.instruction: An owl can turn its head far around without moving its body, because it has twice as many bones as you do in which part?
quests.hint: It connects the head to the body.
quests.explanation: Humans have seven neck bones, and owls have fourteen, which lets them turn their heads about three quarters of the way around.
quests.funFact: Owls cannot move their eyes in their sockets, so turning the head is how they look around.

quests.instruction: An octopus has three of which organ?
quests.hint: It pumps blood.
quests.explanation: Two hearts pump blood through the gills, and one pumps it around the rest of the body.
quests.funFact: Octopus blood is blue, because it uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen.

quests.instruction: A chameleon can look in two different directions at once. Which of its body parts can move separately like that?
quests.hint: They sit on cone-shaped bumps.
quests.explanation: Each chameleon eye moves on its own, so it can watch for food with one and for danger with the other.
quests.funFact: A chameleon's color changes are mostly about mood and temperature, not hiding.
